title: RAG vs long context vs cache-augmented generation
summary: Three ways to put knowledge in front of a model: retrieve chunks per query, send the whole corpus every time, or preload and cache it. Corpus size, update rate and access model decide.
useIf: You are deciding whether you need a retrieval stack at all, or whether a long prompt or a cached preload is enough.
avoidIf: You would pick on a vendor's context-window headline alone, without testing accuracy at your corpus size and measuring cost per query.

explain.md: **RAG** retrieves a few chunks per query. **Long context (LC)** puts the whole corpus in the prompt on every query. **Cache-augmented generation (CAG)** preloads a small, manageable knowledge set into the context and caches the runtime KV state, so no retrieval step runs per query. The CAG authors claim lower latency and fewer retrieval errors for constrained knowledge bases, and it is not suited to large or fast-changing corpora [[r22]].

**Evidence.** Li et al. found that, when resourced enough, long-context models beat RAG on average, but RAG is much cheaper. Their **Self-Route** sends each query to RAG or LC based on the model's self-reflection and keeps accuracy near LC at lower cost [[r21]]. Anthropic's rule of thumb: a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages, can go straight into the prompt [[r26]].

**Why bigger windows are not free.** Accuracy is best when evidence sits at the start or end of the context and drops in the middle [[r24]]. NoLiMa tested 13 models at 32K tokens: 11 fell below 50% of their short-context baseline, and GPT-4o went from 99.3% to 69.7% [[r23]]. Chroma's Context Rot report (2025-07-14) found 18 LLMs less reliable as input grew, even on simple tasks [[r25]].

explain.title: Pick how to supply knowledge
explain.prompt: Flip the dials to see which approach wins and why.

fits.why: No retrieval stage to lose evidence, but tokens are paid every query.

big.why: It does not fit, and accuracy drops with length.

stable.why: Works, with full token cost unless cached.

peruser.why: Assemble each user's documents, at high token cost.

fits.why: A small manageable corpus is its design case [[r22]].

stable.why: Stable content keeps the cache valid.

fast.why: Every update invalidates the cached state.

peruser.why: A shared cache cannot hide documents per user (reasoned limit).

explain.takeaway: Corpus size and update rate pick the family. Per-user access pushes you toward retrieval with filters. Mixed workloads can add a Self-Route style router on top.

whereToUse: A small product manual or policy set that rarely changes, where CAG or a cached prompt can replace a pipeline
A large, changing knowledge base where retrieval stays necessary
Assistants with a mixed workload of lookups and whole-corpus summaries, where routing helps
Prototypes that should test a long prompt before building retrieval

use: Test a long or cached prompt first when the corpus is under about 200,000 tokens and stable
Use RAG when the corpus is large, changing or permissioned
Use routing when workloads split between lookups and global questions
Measure accuracy at your corpus size, not on a vendor benchmark
avoid: Stuffing a large corpus because the window allows it, without measuring accuracy
CAG for fast-changing or per-user corpora
RAG for a tiny stable corpus where it only adds failure points

Corpus passes the window: move to RAG
Per-query token cost dominates: cache the prefix or retrieve
Questions need the whole corpus at once: consider a graph or tree index

pitfalls.symptom: Accuracy falls as the prompt grows, though the facts are present
pitfalls.cause: Position effects and long-context degradation: evidence in the middle is used less [[r24]]
pitfalls.fix: Order evidence at the start or end, shrink the context, or retrieve

pitfalls.symptom: Users see answers about documents they cannot access
pitfalls.cause: A shared cached context contains documents for every role
pitfalls.fix: Use security-filtered retrieval, or one cache per permission scope

scenarios.title: One product manual, twice a year
scenarios.situation: A team supports one 120,000-token manual set. It is revised twice a year and every customer-facing agent may read all of it.
unknowns: Does the platform offer prompt caching?
scenarios.question: How do you supply the manual?

options.name: Preload and cache it (CAG or a cached prompt) and measure accuracy against a RAG baseline
options.why: It is the design case for CAG: small, stable, shared knowledge, with no retrieval stage to lose evidence [[r22]].
options.tradeoff: Revisit when the manual grows or access becomes per role.

options.name: Full hybrid RAG with a reranker
options.tradeoff: More components than this corpus needs today.

options.name: Send the manual uncached on every query
options.why: You pay full token cost each time for content that never changes.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for a prototype or very low volume.

flips.if: The manual grows beyond the window
Different customers may read different manuals
flips.then: Use RAG with security filters, or one cache per permission scope, since a shared cache would leak content.

scenarios.takeaway: Small, stable and shared favours preload and cache.

scenarios.title: Three million tokens, edited daily
scenarios.situation: A wiki of about three million tokens changes every day. Employees see different spaces.
scenarios.question: Which approach?

options.name: Hybrid RAG with incremental indexing and security filters
options.why: Size, update rate and permissions each point to retrieval.
options.tradeoff: Pipeline, ACL sync and retrieval failures to monitor.

options.name: CAG with a nightly rebuilt cache
options.why: It does not fit the window, goes stale daily and a shared cache cannot hide documents.
options.tradeoff: Right for a small, stable, shared corpus.

options.name: Long context with the user's visible pages
options.tradeoff: Does not fit and degrades with length.

flips.if: Questions ask for themes across the whole wiki
flips.then: Add a graph or tree index for those.

flips.if: The wiki shrinks to a small, stable set of public pages
flips.then: Preloading with a cache becomes viable, and simple RAG is still the safer default if updates continue.

scenarios.takeaway: Large, changing and permissioned means retrieval.

scenarios.title: Mixed lookups and whole-document tasks
scenarios.situation: An assistant over a 400,000-token legal binder handles 80% quick lookups and 20% 'summarise everything about clause X' tasks. Cost per query matters.
unknowns: Can a router classify queries reliably?
How long can the model's window stay accurate?
scenarios.question: How do you split the work?

options.name: Route per query: RAG for lookups and a cached long-context pass for whole-document tasks, validated on a golden set
options.why: Self-Route shows routing keeps accuracy near LC at lower cost [[r21]], and the stable binder suits a cached prefix.
options.tradeoff: A router to maintain and two paths to test.

options.name: Long context for every query
options.why: Cost scales with volume, and accuracy drops with length [[r23]].
options.tradeoff: Fine for a few high-value queries a day.

options.name: RAG for everything
options.tradeoff: Whole-document tasks miss evidence outside top-k.

flips.then: Fall back to RAG with a larger k for the global tasks.

flips.if: Nearly all queries become whole-document tasks
flips.then: Use the cached long-context pass as the default and keep RAG only for quick lookups.

quiz.q: A team proposes CAG for HR policies where each employee may see a different subset. What is the main problem?
options: A shared cached context cannot hide documents per user
quiz.explain: A shared preloaded context contains every document, so per-user trimming is impossible. This is a reasoned limit. Use security-filtered retrieval instead.

quiz.q: A 150,000-token corpus is sent uncached on every query. A RAG pipeline sends 6,000 tokens per query. How many times more input tokens does the long-context design send per query?
quiz.explain: 150,000 / 6,000 = 25 times as many input tokens. Prompt caching would discount the repeated prefix, which changes cost but not the accuracy risks of long contexts.

flashcards.back: Preload a small, manageable knowledge set into the context and cache its KV state, so no retrieval runs per query.
Routes each query to RAG or long context based on model self-reflection, keeping accuracy near long context at lower cost.

flashcards.front: What did NoLiMa find at 32K tokens?
flashcards.back: 11 of 13 models fell below 50% of their short-context baseline. GPT-4o dropped from 99.3% to 69.7%.
